title: Isa in the Qur'an's telling
hookLine: the Qur'an says Isa was not killed but raised to Allah, and calls him a word and a spirit from Him (4:157–158; 4:171)

cards: Jesus, in Arabic, is Isa. Some people meet him in the Qur'an for the first time and are surprised at what they find. The Qur'an calls him the Messiah, al-Masih.
His mother Maryam has a surah named for her. Muslims say peace be upon him after his name, as they do for the other prophets.
Near the end of an-Nisa, two short passages give the Qur'an's own account of who he was, and of how his life on earth ended.

teach.h: THEY SLEW HIM NOT, IN THE QUR'AN'S TELLING
teach.b: The first passage, 4:157, answers a claim made by some in his day, that they had killed the Messiah. In Pickthall's words: "They slew him not nor crucified him, but it appeared so unto them."
And 4:158: God raised him up to Himself. The common Muslim reading is that Isa was not crucified, and that God took him up alive. How it appeared so has been explained in different ways.

One classical explanation is that someone else was made to look like him. Other commentators said only that the matter was made to seem so, without naming how. Some Muslim thinkers have read the verse differently again.
And hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari speak of Isa returning before the end of time. Christians believe Jesus was crucified, died, and rose again, and that event is at the center of their faith.
Here the two traditions differ plainly, and each holds its account with deep conviction. The second passage, 4:171, says who Isa is.

teach.h: KALIMAH: A WORD; RUH: A SPIRIT
teach.b: In Pickthall's words: "The Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, was only a messenger of Allah, and His word which He conveyed unto Mary, and a spirit from Him."

teach.h: HIS WORD WHICH HE CONVEYED UNTO MARY.
teach.b: A word, kalimah. Muslims commonly explain it by 3:59: like Adam, he was created by God's word, be, and he was. A spirit from Him, ruh minhu.

The same verse asks the People of the Scripture not to say three, and Christians, who understand the Trinity as one God, have long discussed this verse with Muslims. Both traditions call him the Messiah.
Both call him a word. They mean different things by it, and it's worth knowing exactly what each one means.

how: Muslims honor Isa as a prophet and the Messiah, born of the virgin Maryam; the common Muslim reading of 4:157–158 is that he was not crucified but raised alive to God, hadith speak of his return before the end of time, and Muslims say 'peace be upon him' after his name.

games.why: messenger, word and spirit. Muslims commonly read 'word' through 3:59: created like Adam, by God's word, be.

practice: Sit with the two phrases: a word from Him, a spirit from Him. Don't try to settle anything; just notice what it means that a person can be called a word.
If you have Christian friends, let the deep love they hold for him, in their own way, sit in the same quiet.
